## 1. Introduction

The purpose of this project is to investigate which technical
skills are most valued by employers hiring data science
professionals.

Our group examined LinkedIn job posting data from 2023
and 2024 to identify frequently requested skills such as
Python, SQL, R, machine learning, Tableau, Power BI, and
cloud computing.

We also compared skill requirements across data analysts,
data scientists, and data engineers.

Our analysis included data cleaning, relational database
management using SQLite, exploratory data analysis, and
data visualizations in R.

Our main research question is:

**Which data science skills are most valued by employers?**

## 2. Loading Required Libraries

We used R packages to import, clean, organize, store, and
analyze our data. These packages also allowed us to create
visualizations and manage our relational database.


```{r setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Load the libraries needed for this project

library(tidyverse)
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(readxl)
library(knitr)
```

## 5. Data Cleaning and Quality Checks

Before performing our analysis, we examined the dataset for
missing values and duplicate records. This helped us understand
the quality of the data and identify what needed to be cleaned.

We also reviewed the job titles and experience levels to
make sure the information was consistent before creating our
relational database.

### 5.1 Checking Missing Values

```{r missing-values}
# Count missing values in each column

missing_values <- data_jobs %>%
  summarise(across(
    everything(),
    ~ sum(is.na(.))
  ))

# Display the results
knitr::kable(missing_values)
```


### 5.2 Checking Duplicate Records

```{r check-duplicates}
# Check the number of duplicate job IDs

duplicate_jobs <- sum(duplicated(data_jobs$job_id))

# Display the result
duplicate_jobs
```


### 5.3 Reviewing Experience Levels

```{r experience-levels}
# Count job postings by experience level

experience_summary <- data_jobs %>%
  count(formatted_experience_level, sort = TRUE)

# Display the results
knitr::kable(experience_summary)
```

### 5.4 Cleaning and Standardizing the Data

After reviewing the missing values and experience levels,
we prepared the dataset for our analysis. We
remove duplicate job IDs, standardize the job categories,
and label missing experience levels as "Not Specified."

We kept records with missing skill descriptions
because we used supplementary skill data from
Kaggle.


```{r clean-job-data}
# Clean and standardize the job posting data

data_jobs_clean <- data_jobs %>%
  distinct(job_id, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    job_category = case_when(
      str_detect(str_to_lower(title), "data scientist") ~ "Data Scientist",
      str_detect(str_to_lower(title), "data engineer") ~ "Data Engineer",
      str_detect(str_to_lower(title), "data analyst") ~ "Data Analyst",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    ),
    experience_level = if_else(
      is.na(formatted_experience_level),
      "Not Specified",
      formatted_experience_level
    )
  )

# Check the cleaned job categories
data_jobs_clean %>%
  count(job_category)

# Confirm the total number of records
nrow(data_jobs_clean)
```

## 6. Creating a Relational Database

We used SQLite to organize our cleaned job posting data into
normalized relational tables. Instead of storing the same company
and location information repeatedly, we separated the data
into related tables and connect them using primary and foreign keys.

We used the DBI and RSQLite packages to create and manage
our database.


### 6.1 Setting Up the Database

```{r create-database}

# Create the database folder
dir.create("database", showWarnings = FALSE)

# Create the database connection
con <- dbConnect(
  SQLite(),
  "database/data_science_skills.sqlite"
)

# Enable foreign key constraints
dbExecute(con, "PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON")

# Remove existing tables before rebuilding
# Delete child tables before parent tables
dbExecute(con, "DROP TABLE IF EXISTS Posting_Skills")
dbExecute(con, "DROP TABLE IF EXISTS Skills")
dbExecute(con, "DROP TABLE IF EXISTS Job_Postings")
dbExecute(con, "DROP TABLE IF EXISTS Locations")
dbExecute(con, "DROP TABLE IF EXISTS Companies")

# Verify connection
dbIsValid(con)
```

### 6.2 Creating Normalized Relational Tables

We separated the cleaned job posting data into
relational tables for companies, locations, and job postings.

The Companies table stores company information, while
the Locations table stores unique job locations.
The Job_Postings table contains the individual postings
and connect them to the other tables using foreign keys.

This structure reduces repeated information and help
maintain consistency in our database.


```{r create-companies-table}
# Create a table containing unique companies

companies <- data_jobs_clean %>%
  filter(!is.na(company_name)) %>%
  distinct(company_name) %>%
  arrange(company_name) %>%
  mutate(company_key = row_number()) %>%
  select(company_key, company_name)

# Create the Companies table with a primary key
dbExecute(con, "
  CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS Companies (
    company_key INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    company_name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE
  )
")

# Insert company records
dbWriteTable(
  con,
  "Companies",
  companies,
  append = TRUE
)

# Check the records
head(companies)
```

```{r create-locations-table}
# Create a table containing unique locations

locations <- data_jobs_clean %>%
  filter(!is.na(location)) %>%
  distinct(location) %>%
  arrange(location) %>%
  mutate(location_key = row_number()) %>%
  select(location_key, location)

# Create the Locations table with a primary key
dbExecute(con, "
  CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS Locations (
    location_key INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    location TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE
  )
")

# Insert location records
dbWriteTable(
  con,
  "Locations",
  locations,
  append = TRUE
)

# Check the records
head(locations)
```

```{r create-job-postings-table}
# Connect job postings with the company and location tables

job_postings <- data_jobs_clean %>%
  left_join(companies, by = "company_name") %>%
  left_join(locations, by = "location") %>%
  transmute(
    job_id = as.character(job_id),
    company_key,
    location_key,
    title,
    job_category,
    experience_level
  )

# Create the Job_Postings table with foreign keys
dbExecute(con, "
  CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS Job_Postings (
    job_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    company_key INTEGER,
    location_key INTEGER,
    title TEXT,
    job_category TEXT,
    experience_level TEXT,
    FOREIGN KEY (company_key)
      REFERENCES Companies(company_key),
    FOREIGN KEY (location_key)
      REFERENCES Locations(location_key)
  )
")

# Insert job posting records
dbWriteTable(
  con,
  "Job_Postings",
  job_postings,
  append = TRUE
)

# Preview the records
head(job_postings)
```

### 6.3 Checking Database Tables

```{r verify-database}
# List the tables created in SQLite
dbListTables(con)

# Count records stored in each table
dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT 'Companies' AS table_name, COUNT(*) AS records
  FROM Companies
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 'Locations', COUNT(*)
  FROM Locations
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 'Job_Postings', COUNT(*)
  FROM Job_Postings
")
```

### 6.4 Verifying Database Relationships

After creating the relational tables, we checked whether the
job postings can be connected to their company and location
information.

We used SQL JOIN statements to retrieve information from
multiple tables. This helps us confirm that our primary
and foreign keys are working correctly.


```{r verify-table-relationships}
# Join job postings with companies and locations

joined_jobs <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT
    j.job_id,
    j.title,
    j.job_category,
    c.company_name,
    l.location,
    j.experience_level
  FROM Job_Postings AS j
  LEFT JOIN Companies AS c
    ON j.company_key = c.company_key
  LEFT JOIN Locations AS l
    ON j.location_key = l.location_key
  LIMIT 10
")

# Display the results
knitr::kable(joined_jobs)
```

```{r check-foreign-keys}
# Check for foreign key violations

foreign_key_check <- dbGetQuery(
  con,
  "PRAGMA foreign_key_check"
)

# Display results
foreign_key_check
```

## 7. Importing and Organizing Skill Data

We imported two additional files from the LinkedIn dataset.
The job_skills.csv file connects job postings with skill codes,
while skills.csv provides the names of those skill categories.

We matched the skill records to our filtered job postings
and prepare them for our relational database.

### 7.1 Importing the Supplementary Files

```{r import-skills-data}
# Import the supplementary LinkedIn datasets from GitHub

job_skills <- read_csv(
  paste0(data_url, "job_skills.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE,
  col_types = cols(job_id = col_character())
)

skills <- read_csv(
  paste0(data_url, "skills.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Check the dataset dimensions
dim(job_skills)
dim(skills)

# Preview the files
head(job_skills)
head(skills)
```

### 7.2 Matching Skills to Job Postings

We matched job IDs from the skill dataset with the job IDs
in our cleaned job posting dataset. This allows us to keep
only the skill records relevant to our research.

We also checked for duplicate relationships and confirmed
that the skill codes have matching descriptions.


```{r match-job-skills}

# Keep only skills associated with our cleaned jobs
job_skills_filtered <- job_skills %>%
  semi_join(
    data_jobs_clean %>%
      select(job_id),
    by = "job_id"
  ) %>%
  distinct(job_id, skill_abr)

# Match skill codes with their category names
job_skills_named <- job_skills_filtered %>%
  left_join(skills, by = "skill_abr")

# Verify the matched records
nrow(job_skills_filtered)
n_distinct(job_skills_filtered$job_id)

# Check missing skill names
sum(is.na(job_skills_named$skill_name))

# Preview the results
knitr::kable(head(job_skills_named, 10))
```

### 7.3 Creating the Skills and Posting_Skills Tables

We created two additional relational tables in SQLite.
The Skills table stores unique skill categories, while the
Posting_Skills table connects job postings with their
associated skill categories.

This establishes a many-to-many relationship between job
postings and skills while reducing duplicate information.


```{r create-skills-table}
# Create a table of unique skill categories

skills_table <- skills %>%
  distinct(skill_abr, skill_name) %>%
  filter(!is.na(skill_abr), !is.na(skill_name))

# Create the Skills table
dbExecute(con, "
  CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS Skills (
    skill_abr TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    skill_name TEXT NOT NULL
  )
")

# Insert the skill categories
dbWriteTable(
  con,
  "Skills",
  skills_table,
  append = TRUE
)

# Verify the number of records
dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_skills FROM Skills")
```

```{r create-posting-skills-table}
# Prepare the linking table

posting_skills_table <- job_skills_filtered %>%
  distinct(job_id, skill_abr) %>%
  filter(!is.na(job_id), !is.na(skill_abr))

# Create the many-to-many linking table
dbExecute(con, "
  CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS Posting_Skills (
    job_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    skill_abr TEXT NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (job_id, skill_abr),
    FOREIGN KEY (job_id) REFERENCES Job_Postings(job_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (skill_abr) REFERENCES Skills(skill_abr)
  )
")

# Insert the matching records
dbWriteTable(
  con,
  "Posting_Skills",
  posting_skills_table,
  append = TRUE
)

# Check the total relationships
dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_relationships
  FROM Posting_Skills
")
```

```{r verify-all-tables}
# Display all database tables
dbListTables(con)

# Check the number of records in each table
table_summary <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT 'Companies' AS table_name, COUNT(*) AS records FROM Companies
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 'Locations', COUNT(*) FROM Locations
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 'Job_Postings', COUNT(*) FROM Job_Postings
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 'Skills', COUNT(*) FROM Skills
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 'Posting_Skills', COUNT(*) FROM Posting_Skills
")

knitr::kable(table_summary)

# Check for broken foreign key references
dbGetQuery(con, "PRAGMA foreign_key_check")
```

## 8. Exploratory Data Analysis

We used exploratory data analysis to examine patterns in the
LinkedIn job posting dataset. Our goal is to identify which skill
categories appear most frequently and compare how these
requirements vary across data science job roles.

We used SQL to retrieve information from our relational
database and R to summarize and visualize the results.


### 8.1 Calculating Skill Category Demand

```{r skill-frequency-analysis}
# Calculate the frequency of each skill category

skill_frequency <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT
    s.skill_name,
    COUNT(DISTINCT ps.job_id) AS job_count
  FROM Posting_Skills AS ps
  INNER JOIN Skills AS s
    ON ps.skill_abr = s.skill_abr
  GROUP BY s.skill_name
  ORDER BY job_count DESC
")

# Calculate percentages using all 1,052 postings
skill_frequency <- skill_frequency %>%
  mutate(
    percentage = round(job_count / nrow(data_jobs_clean) * 100, 1)
  )

# Display the results
knitr::kable(skill_frequency)
```

### 8.2 Visualizing Skill Category Demand

To better understand which skill categories appear most frequently
in the LinkedIn job postings, we created a horizontal bar chart.

The chart displays the percentage of job postings associated
with each skill category. This helps us identify the most
common skill requirements and make comparisons between categories.

We used ggplot2 to create the visualization.

```{r skill-frequency-chart}

# Select the 10 most frequently listed skill categories
top_skills <- skill_frequency %>%
  arrange(desc(job_count)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10)

# Create a horizontal bar chart
ggplot(
  top_skills,
  aes(
    x = reorder(skill_name, percentage),
    y = percentage
  )
) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(percentage, "%")),
    hjust = -0.1,
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, max(top_skills$percentage) * 1.15)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Top 10 Skill Categories in Data Science Job Postings",
    subtitle = "LinkedIn job postings (2023–2024)",
    x = "Skill Category",
    y = "Percentage of All Job Postings",
    caption = "Source: Kaggle LinkedIn Job Postings Dataset"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### 8.3 Comparing Skill Categories Across Job Roles

We compared skill category requirements across Data Analyst,
Data Scientist, and Data Engineer positions.

This analysis helps us identify differences in employer
requirements based on job role. We calculated the percentage
of postings mentioning each skill category within each role.


```{r skill-categories-by-role}
# Calculate skill category demand by job role

role_skill_summary <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT
    j.job_category,
    s.skill_name,
    COUNT(DISTINCT ps.job_id) AS job_count
  FROM Job_Postings AS j
  INNER JOIN Posting_Skills AS ps
    ON j.job_id = ps.job_id
  INNER JOIN Skills AS s
    ON ps.skill_abr = s.skill_abr
  GROUP BY j.job_category, s.skill_name
")

# Calculate total postings in each job category
role_totals <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT
    job_category,
    COUNT(*) AS total_jobs
  FROM Job_Postings
  GROUP BY job_category
")

# Calculate percentages within each job category
role_skill_summary <- role_skill_summary %>%
  left_join(role_totals, by = "job_category") %>%
  mutate(
    percentage = round(job_count / total_jobs * 100, 1)
  )

# Display the results
knitr::kable(head(role_skill_summary, 15))
```

### 8.4 Visualizing Skill Categories by Job Role

We created a grouped bar chart to compare skill categories
across Data Analyst, Data Scientist, and Data Engineer positions.

This helps us identify how frequently different skill
categories appear within each job role and highlight
differences in employer requirements.


```{r compare-skills-by-role}
# Select the five most common skill categories overall

top_five_skills <- skill_frequency %>%
  arrange(desc(job_count)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5) %>%
  pull(skill_name)

# Filter the role comparison data
role_skill_plot <- role_skill_summary %>%
  filter(skill_name %in% top_five_skills) %>%
  select(job_category, skill_name, percentage)

# Create a grouped bar chart
ggplot(
  role_skill_plot,
  aes(
    x = skill_name,
    y = percentage,
    fill = job_category
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.8),
    width = 0.7
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Skill Categories by Data Science Job Role",
    subtitle = "Comparison of Data Analyst, Data Scientist, and Data Engineer",
    x = "Skill Category",
    y = "Percentage of Postings Within Each Role",
    fill = "Job Role",
    caption = "Source: Kaggle LinkedIn Job Postings (2023–2024)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## 9. Identifying Specific Technical Skills

Although the supplementary skill files provide general skill
categories, our research focuses on specific technical skills.

We examined job descriptions to identify mentions of
technologies such as Python, SQL, R, machine learning, Tableau,
Power BI, and cloud platforms.

This allows us to compare technical skill requirements
across different data science job roles.

### 9.1 Checking Available Job Descriptions

```{r check-job-descriptions}
# Check whether the original dataset is available
exists("postings")

# Check whether it contains job descriptions
if (exists("postings")) {
  "description" %in% names(postings)
}
```

### 9.2 Preparing Job Descriptions

We originally extracted job descriptions from the LinkedIn
dataset and matched them to our 1,052 selected job postings.

We saved the smaller file to GitHub so our group could access
the descriptions without downloading the entire original dataset.

We used these descriptions to identify specific technical
skills mentioned by employers.


### 9.3 Importing Job Descriptions from GitHub

We imported the filtered job descriptions from our GitHub
repository. This allows us to analyze technical skills using
the same dataset without requiring other group members to
download the original large CSV file.


```{r import-job-descriptions}

# Import job descriptions from GitHub
job_descriptions <- read_csv(
  paste0(data_url, "job_descriptions.csv"),
  col_types = cols(
    job_id = col_character(),
    description = col_character()
  )
)

# Verify the number of records
nrow(job_descriptions)

# Check missing descriptions
sum(
  is.na(job_descriptions$description) |
  trimws(job_descriptions$description) == ""
)

# Preview the dataset
job_descriptions %>%
  mutate(description_length = nchar(description)) %>%
  select(job_id, description_length) %>%
  head(10) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

### 9.4 Identifying Technical Skills

We searched job descriptions for mentions of selected
technical skills, including Python, SQL, R, machine learning,
Tableau, Power BI, and cloud technologies.

We used string matching in R to identify whether each
job posting mentions a particular technology. Each skill
was counted only once per posting, even if it appears
multiple times in the description.


```{r identify-technical-skills}

# Define technical skills and search patterns
skill_patterns <- c(
  Python = "\\bpython\\b",
  SQL = "\\bsql\\b",
  R = "\\bR\\b",
  `Machine Learning` = "\\bmachine learning\\b",
  Tableau = "\\btableau\\b",
  `Power BI` = "\\bpower\\s*bi\\b",
  Cloud = "\\b(aws|azure|gcp|google cloud|cloud computing)\\b"
)

# Identify mentions of each skill in job descriptions
technical_skills <- job_descriptions %>%
  mutate(
    across(
      description,
      ~ replace_na(.x, "")
    )
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Python = str_detect(description, regex(skill_patterns["Python"], ignore_case = TRUE)),
    SQL = str_detect(description, regex(skill_patterns["SQL"], ignore_case = TRUE)),
    R = str_detect(description, regex(skill_patterns["R"], ignore_case = FALSE)),
    `Machine Learning` = str_detect(description, regex(skill_patterns["Machine Learning"], ignore_case = TRUE)),
    Tableau = str_detect(description, regex(skill_patterns["Tableau"], ignore_case = TRUE)),
    `Power BI` = str_detect(description, regex(skill_patterns["Power BI"], ignore_case = TRUE)),
    Cloud = str_detect(description, regex(skill_patterns["Cloud"], ignore_case = TRUE))
  )

# Preview results
technical_skills %>%
  select(-description) %>%
  head(10) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

### 9.4.1 Refining R Skill Detection

We identified that some job descriptions reference R&D
(Research and Development), which could be mistaken for
the R programming language.

We removed R&D references from the text before
checking for R programming mentions. This allows us
to retain postings that mention both R&D and R programming.


```{r refine-r-detection}
# Remove R&D references before checking for R

technical_skills <- technical_skills %>%
  mutate(
    description_without_rd = str_remove_all(
      description,
      regex("\\bR\\s*&\\s*D\\b", ignore_case = TRUE)
    ),
    R = str_detect(
      description_without_rd,
      "\\bR\\b"
    )
  )

```

### 9.5 Calculating Technical Skill Demand

We calculated how frequently each technical skill appears
in the job descriptions. Each skill was counted once per
posting, regardless of how many times it is mentioned.

We then calculated the percentage of job postings mentioning
each skill and rank the results to identify which technologies
appear most frequently.


```{r technical-skill-frequency}
# Convert skill detection results into long format

technical_skills_long <- technical_skills %>%
  select(
    job_id, Python, SQL, R,
    `Machine Learning`, Tableau, `Power BI`, Cloud
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -job_id,
    names_to = "skill",
    values_to = "mentioned"
  )

# Calculate technical skill frequencies
technical_skill_frequency <- technical_skills_long %>%
  group_by(skill) %>%
  summarise(
    job_count = sum(mentioned, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    percentage = round(
      job_count / nrow(data_jobs_clean) * 100, 1
    )
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(job_count))

# Display the results
knitr::kable(technical_skill_frequency)
```

### 9.6 Visualizing Technical Skill Demand

We created a bar chart to compare how frequently specific
technical skills appear in the LinkedIn job descriptions.

This visualization helps us identify which technologies
are mentioned most frequently across the selected data-related
job postings.


```{r technical-skills-chart}
# Create a horizontal bar chart of technical skill mentions

ggplot(
  technical_skill_frequency,
  aes(
    x = reorder(skill, percentage),
    y = percentage
  )
) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(percentage, "%")),
    hjust = -0.15,
    size = 4
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, max(technical_skill_frequency$percentage) * 1.15)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Most Frequently Mentioned Technical Skills",
    subtitle = "1,052 LinkedIn Data-Related Job Postings (2023–2024)",
    x = "Technical Skill",
    y = "Percentage of Job Postings",
    caption = "Source: Kaggle LinkedIn Job Postings Dataset"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### 9.7 Validating Technical Skill Detection

We reviewed a sample of job descriptions to check whether
our text-matching method correctly identifies technical skills.

This step is important because some technology names may appear
in different contexts. We focused on verifying R and checking
that our results accurately reflect technology mentions.


```{r validate-technical-skills}
# Review the context surrounding R matches

r_matches <- technical_skills %>%
  filter(R == TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10) %>%
  mutate(
    match_location = str_locate(description, "\\bR\\b")[, 1],

    match_context = str_sub(
      description,
      pmax(1, match_location - 60),
      match_location + 60
    )
  ) %>%
  select(job_id, match_context)

# Display the results
knitr::kable(r_matches)
```

### 9.8 Comparing Technical Skills Across Job Roles

We compared technical skill mentions across Data Analyst,
Data Scientist, and Data Engineer job postings.

This analysis helps us understand whether certain
technologies are mentioned more frequently for specific roles.
We calculated percentages within each job category so
the results can be compared fairly.


```{r compare-technical-skills-by-role}
# Match technical skills with job categories

technical_skills_by_role <- technical_skills %>%
  select(
    job_id, Python, SQL, R,
    `Machine Learning`, Tableau, `Power BI`, Cloud
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    data_jobs_clean %>%
      select(job_id, job_category),
    by = "job_id"
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(
      Python, SQL, R, `Machine Learning`,
      Tableau, `Power BI`, Cloud
    ),
    names_to = "skill",
    values_to = "mentioned"
  )

# Calculate skill frequency within each role
role_technical_summary <- technical_skills_by_role %>%
  filter(!is.na(job_category)) %>%
  group_by(job_category, skill) %>%
  summarise(
    job_count = sum(mentioned, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_jobs = n_distinct(job_id),
    percentage = round(job_count / total_jobs * 100, 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Display the results
knitr::kable(role_technical_summary)
```


### 9.9 Visualizing Technical Skills Across Job Roles

We created a grouped bar chart to compare technical
skill mentions across Data Analyst, Data Scientist, and
Data Engineer positions.

This visualization helps us identify which technologies
are most frequently mentioned for each role and understand
how technical skill requirements differ between occupations.


```{r technical-skills-by-role-chart}
# Create a grouped bar chart comparing technical skills

ggplot(
  role_technical_summary,
  aes(
    x = skill,
    y = percentage,
    fill = job_category
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.8),
    width = 0.7
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 100, 20),
    limits = c(0, 100)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Technical Skill Mentions by Data Science Job Role",
    subtitle = "LinkedIn Job Postings (2023–2024)",
    x = "Technical Skill",
    y = "Percentage of Postings Within Each Role",
    fill = "Job Role",
    caption = "Source: Kaggle LinkedIn Job Postings Dataset"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## 10. Data Quality and Limitations

Our analysis uses LinkedIn job postings from 2023 and 2024.
We selected 1,052 postings associated with Data Analyst,
Data Scientist, and Data Engineer positions.

We identified technical skills by searching job descriptions
for technology names. Although this approach helps us
measure how frequently skills are mentioned, it does not
always indicate whether a skill is required or preferred.

We also identified potential false positives when searching
for the R programming language. We refined our detection
method to reduce incorrect matches involving R&D.

Our findings represent the selected LinkedIn job postings
rather than the entire data science job market. Because
the dataset covers 2023–2024, it may not reflect current
hiring trends.


```{r description-quality-check}
# Count missing and available descriptions

description_quality <- job_descriptions %>%
  summarise(
    total_records = n(),
    missing_descriptions = sum(
      is.na(description) | trimws(description) == ""
    ),
    available_descriptions = total_records - missing_descriptions
  )

knitr::kable(description_quality)
```

## 11. Comparing LinkedIn Findings with O*NET

To provide another perspective on technical skill demand,
we used the O*NET Software Skills dataset as a secondary source.

We selected three occupations related to our LinkedIn job
categories and examined the software technologies associated
with each occupation.

Since LinkedIn and O*NET measure different aspects of skill
demand, we compared the findings separately rather than
treating them as equivalent measurements.

### 11.1 Importing O*NET Software Skills Data

We used the O*NET Software Skills dataset as a secondary
source to compare our LinkedIn findings with occupational
technology information.

We focused on data-related occupations and identify the
software technologies associated with each occupation.


```{r import-onet-data}

# Download the O*NET Excel file from GitHub
onet_url <- paste0(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LBoodram26/",
  "Project-3/Data/Software%20Skills.xlsx"
)

onet_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".xlsx")
download.file(onet_url, onet_file, mode = "wb")

# Import the Excel dataset
onet_skills <- read_excel(onet_file)

# Verify the data
dim(onet_skills)
names(onet_skills)
head(onet_skills)
```

### 11.2 Filtering O*NET Occupations

We filtered the O*NET Software Skills dataset to focus
on occupations related to our LinkedIn job categories.

We selected Data Scientists, Business Intelligence Analysts,
and Database Architects to compare their associated software
technologies.

Although these occupations are related to our research,
they are not all exact matches to the LinkedIn job titles.


```{r filter-onet-occupations}
# Select the O*NET occupations relevant to our project

onet_filtered <- onet_skills %>%
  filter(
    `O*NET-SOC Code` %in% c(
      "15-2051.00",
      "15-2051.01",
      "15-1243.00"
    )
  )

# Count software entries for each occupation
onet_occupation_summary <- onet_filtered %>%
  count(
    `O*NET-SOC Code`,
    Title,
    name = "software_count"
  )

# Display the results
knitr::kable(onet_occupation_summary)

# Confirm the total filtered records
nrow(onet_filtered)
```

### 11.3 Identifying Technical Skills in O*NET

We examined the software technologies listed in O*NET
for Data Scientists, Business Intelligence Analysts, and
Database Architects.

We looked for technologies related to Python, SQL, R,
machine learning, Tableau, Power BI, and cloud platforms.

This analysis helps us compare our LinkedIn findings
with an independent occupational data source.


```{r identify-onet-skills}

# Define technology search patterns
onet_patterns <- c(
  Python = "\\bpython\\b",
  SQL = "\\bsql\\b",
  R = "\\bR\\b",
  `Machine Learning` = "machine learning",
  Tableau = "tableau",
  `Power BI` = "power\\s*bi",
  Cloud = "\\b(aws|azure|google cloud|gcp)\\b"
)

# Search O*NET software examples for these technologies
onet_technical_skills <- onet_filtered %>%
  mutate(
    software_name = replace_na(`Workplace Example`, ""),
    Python = str_detect(
      software_name,
      regex(onet_patterns["Python"], ignore_case = TRUE)
    ),
    SQL = str_detect(
      software_name,
      regex(onet_patterns["SQL"], ignore_case = TRUE)
    ),
    R = str_detect(
      software_name,
      "\\bR\\b"
    ),
    `Machine Learning` = str_detect(
      software_name,
      regex(onet_patterns["Machine Learning"], ignore_case = TRUE)
    ),
    Tableau = str_detect(
      software_name,
      regex(onet_patterns["Tableau"], ignore_case = TRUE)
    ),
    `Power BI` = str_detect(
      software_name,
      regex(onet_patterns["Power BI"], ignore_case = TRUE)
    ),
    Cloud = str_detect(
      software_name,
      regex(onet_patterns["Cloud"], ignore_case = TRUE)
    )
  )

# Display the matching software entries
onet_matches <- onet_technical_skills %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(
      Python, SQL, R, `Machine Learning`,
      Tableau, `Power BI`, Cloud
    ),
    names_to = "technical_skill",
    values_to = "mentioned"
  ) %>%
  filter(mentioned) %>%
  select(
    Title,
    `Workplace Example`,
    technical_skill,
    `In Demand`
  )

knitr::kable(head(onet_matches, 20))
```

### 11.4 Summarizing O*NET Technical Skills

We summarized the technologies identified in O*NET
for the three selected occupations.

We examined which technologies are listed for each
occupation and how many matching software entries are
identified as in demand.

This provides an independent comparison with our
LinkedIn job posting analysis.


```{r summarize-onet-skills}
# Summarize O*NET technology matches by occupation

onet_skill_summary <- onet_matches %>%
  group_by(Title, technical_skill) %>%
  summarise(
    software_entries = n_distinct(`Workplace Example`),
    in_demand_entries = n_distinct(
      `Workplace Example`[`In Demand` == "Y"]
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(Title, desc(in_demand_entries))

# Display the summary
knitr::kable(onet_skill_summary)
```

### 11.5 Comparing LinkedIn and O*NET Findings

We compared the technical skills identified in LinkedIn job
descriptions with technologies identified in O*NET.

LinkedIn measures how frequently skills are mentioned in our
sample of job postings, while O*NET identifies software
technologies associated with occupations and indicates whether
individual technologies are classified as in demand.

We used O*NET as a secondary reference rather than directly
comparing its software-entry counts with LinkedIn percentages.


```{r compare-linkedin-onet}
# Summarize whether O*NET identifies in-demand software
# in each selected technical skill group

onet_comparison <- onet_skill_summary %>%
  group_by(technical_skill) %>%
  summarise(
    occupations_listed = n_distinct(Title),
    occupations_in_demand = n_distinct(
      Title[in_demand_entries > 0]
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Combine with LinkedIn technical skill percentages
comparison_table <- technical_skill_frequency %>%
  left_join(
    onet_comparison,
    by = c("skill" = "technical_skill")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    occupations_listed = replace_na(
      occupations_listed, 0L
    ),
    occupations_in_demand = replace_na(
      occupations_in_demand, 0L
    )
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(percentage))

# Display comparison
knitr::kable(
  comparison_table,
  col.names = c(
    "Technical Skill",
    "LinkedIn Job Count",
    "LinkedIn %",
    "O*NET Occupations Listed",
    "O*NET Occupations In Demand"
  )
)
```

## 12. Findings and Conclusions

### 12.1 Main Findings

The goal of this project was to understand which technical
skills are most frequently mentioned in data-related job
postings and whether those skills differ across job roles.

We analyzed 1,052 LinkedIn job postings from 2023 and 2024,
focusing on Data Analyst, Data Scientist, and Data Engineer
positions.

SQL was the most common technical skill overall, appearing in
63.8% of postings and in at least 59% of postings for each
job role. Cloud technologies stood out in Data Engineer
postings (73.6%), compared with Data Scientist (33.6%) and
Data Analyst (12.3%) postings.

Python (85.4%) and machine learning (71.3%) were mentioned
more frequently than R (55.1%) in Data Scientist postings.
R was mentioned less frequently in Data Analyst (14.3%) and
Data Engineer (3.8%) postings.

### 12.2 O*NET Comparison

We used the O*NET Software Skills dataset as a second source
to compare our findings.

O*NET identified SQL, Python, Tableau, Power BI, and cloud
technologies as having in-demand software entries across
the three occupations we selected.

Although O*NET measures occupational software associations
rather than the percentage of job postings, it provided
additional context for our LinkedIn findings.

### 12.3 Limitations

For the O*NET comparison, we selected occupations that were
closely related to our LinkedIn job categories, but they were
not all exact matches. Additionally, our technology matching
method may not identify every relevant software product,
particularly those used for machine learning.

Our analysis was based on a selected group of LinkedIn job
postings from 2023 and 2024, so the results may not represent
all employers or current hiring trends.

We identified skills through text matching, which means
some references could be missed or incorrectly identified.
We also measured skill mentions rather than confirming
whether a technology was required or preferred.


### 12.4 Conclusion

Based on our analysis, SQL and Python were the most frequently
mentioned technical skills overall. However, different job
roles emphasized different technologies.

These findings suggest that people entering the data field
should consider the requirements of their intended role
when deciding which technical skills to develop.
